hints: Focus on the word always. Ask yourself which of these three molecules can vary in structure and which has a fixed minimum number of bonds.
Count the C=O double bonds in the linkages: a triglyceride always has 3 ester bonds, while proteins always have very many peptide bond C=O groups plus haem adds more.
walkthrough:
**Understand what always means**

Think like a detective. We are not asking if it can have four double bonds, we are asking if it must have four or more every time.

A saturated molecule with no C=C bonds is the test case.

**Check triglyceride first**

A triglyceride is glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by 3 ester bonds.

Each ester bond contains one C=O double bond, so the backbone gives exactly 3 double bonds:
$$3 \text{ ester bonds} = 3 \times \text{C=O} = 3 \text{ double bonds}$$
A fully saturated triglyceride has no C=C in its tails, so it has only 3. It does not always reach four.

**Check the two proteins**

Collagen and haemoglobin are both very large proteins made of hundreds of amino acids.

Every peptide bond linking two amino acids contains a C=O double bond, so a protein with hundreds of bonds has hundreds of double bonds. Haemoglobin has even more because each of its 4 haem groups contains a porphyrin ring full of conjugated C=C and C=N double bonds.

Both proteins therefore always have far more than four double bonds, so the correct pair is haemoglobin and collagen only.

options.A: Incorrect because triglyceride does not qualify. A saturated triglyceride has only the 3 C=O bonds from its 3 ester links.
options.B: Incorrect because triglyceride does not qualify, even though collagen does with its hundreds of peptide bond C=O groups.
options.C: Correct. Both are large proteins with hundreds of peptide C=O double bonds, and haemoglobin has extra double bonds in its 4 haem groups.
options.D: Incorrect because triglyceride does not qualify, even though haemoglobin does with its peptide bonds and haem ring double bonds.
